entry.title: US Patent 12,541,676 — Neurometric Authentication System
entry.content:
Background and inspiration

This is my first patent, and it carries the same name as the work it grew out of. Out of the paranoia I was gifted from SPQR I set out to design an end to end secure BCI. It begged the question: what is secure, what is an interface, and what is the root chain we can trust as “intention”.

Process

The build-out beyond the publication included two major additions:

Macro commands. M measured neurological impulse resolves to N^M macro commands where N is the resolution of (or number of symbols in) the BCI’s language.

Intention as the identifier. The thing that distinguishes one user of the device from another is not a stored credential but the shape of the intention itself - a derived “mind-print”, constantly verified.

The described system of systems allows for multimodal acquisition, the security guarantees of an isolated air-gapped verification path, and implied ingenious UIs built on top.

The claimed pipeline runs: sensors generate voltage signals from a measured neurological impulse → ASICs digitize them → an activation command wakes the device from an energy-efficient mode into an active mode → the signal is encoded from the time domain into the frequency domain (via FFT or Riemannian geometry) → a support-vector machine or convolutional neural network classifies it → the resulting macro command is encoded into a token alongside verification data derived from a random seed → the token is broadcast, and the destination device verifies it with a server before acting.

Result

  • Patent number: US 12,541,676 B2
  • Title: Neurometric authentication system
  • Inventor: Angel Raphael Rodriguez (sole)
  • Priority date: January 20, 2020
  • Filed: January 20, 2021
  • Published as application: US 2021/0224637 A1, July 22, 2021
  • Granted: February 3, 2026

Read on Google Patents

entry.title: Trick or Heat? Attacking Temperature Control With a Radio

link.title: Trick or Heat? Attacking Temperature Control With a Radio

entry.content:
Background and inspiration

In the summer of 2018 I decided to give myself a shot at my dream of being a scientist and a researcher. I had okay grades and, from my perspective, no experience. I applied to the position anyway.

When I got the interview with Dr. Sara Rampazzi I was surprised, nervous, and afterward certain I had not gotten it.

I count taking that chance as another one of my “greatest accomplishments” — because I never expected that a single choice would produce my greatest friends, my greatest times, and many more of my greatest accomplishments.

I was hired to conduct laboratory experiments in the SPQR Lab at the University of Michigan College of Engineering.

Process

The idea was simple. Wires, traces, and conductors carry a measurable induced current in a changing magnetic field. Your microwave messes with the TV. Your cell phone messes with your speakers. And if you have ever worked with raw signals, you know that noise filtering is a front-loaded expectation before you can extract anything useful at all.

So: what if we intentionally fire radio waves into sensitive sensors?

And further — if that sensors’ system is guiding logic, can we gain the ability to exploit the logic itself?

No code. Just a walkie-talkie and physics.

My role on the project:

  • Running the “walkie” — a USRP software-defined radio
  • Building our sensor system test bed
  • Writing sections of the paper, and reviewing others
  • Coordinating between our lab partners across two universities
  • Presenting the idea for the mitigation system, and collaborating on its refinement

Result

The work became a paper at ACM CCS 2019 in London. We showed that an adversary can remotely manipulate the temperature readings of a critical system — an infant incubator among them — by inducing an unintended rectification effect in the operational and instrumentation amplifiers that condition the sensor signal. The control loop heats or cools on command, without the attacker touching the device. The same hardware-level weakness reaches other classes of sensors that share a similar signal conditioning path. Because conventional defenses were not enough, we proposed a low-cost anomaly detector to protect the integrity of the sensor signal.

Yazhou Tu, Sara Rampazzi, Bin Hao, Angel Rodriguez, Kevin Fu, and Xiali Hei. “Trick or Heat? Manipulating Critical Temperature-Based Control Systems Using Rectification Attacks.” Proceedings of the 2019 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS ‘19), London, United Kingdom, pp. 2301–2315.

ACM Digital Library Preprint (arXiv)

Where my head’s at now

This was my first paper, and I loved it. It is also the project that permanently changed how I look at a embedded systems: the specified behavior on the datasheet of components is a narrowed description of the system, guessed (see: industry) and under ideal conditions.
entry.summary: My first paper. No code, just a software-defined radio and physics — and what happens when the sensor feeding a control loop can be told what to say.

entry.title: Light Commands: A Fly on the Wall

link.title: Light Commands: A Fly on the Wall

entry.content:
Background and inspiration

Light Commands is the discovery that you can inject voice commands into a smart speaker or phone by pointing a modulated laser at its microphone — no sound, no proximity, no code on the device. The MEMS microphone responds to light as though it were sound.

I dare not take anything away from the massive efforts of Dr. Benjamin Cyr and Dr. Sara Rampazzi on this project. I was honored to be a fly on the wall throughout the process.

Process

My contribution here was presence and a camera. All of the photographs on the project’s website were taken by me.

What I witnessed was science and beautiful raw human effort, ingenuity, and dedication.

Result

entry.title: IoT Two-Factor Neurometric Authentication Using Wearable EEG

link.title: IoT Two-Factor Neurometric Authentication Using Wearable EEG

entry.content:
Background and inspiration

I loved the idea of interfacing directly with a computer — human expansion, the entity of our will wrapping around us like an exosuit and reaching into the digital ocean. Ghost in the Shell. Mechas. Iron Man. The Jaegers in Pacific Rim.

An early dream was to build technology that enabled that. But every version of it was contingent on two marvels of engineering: fusion, and brain-computer interfaces.

So when I sought out and received the opportunity to lead my own publication, I knew it would be about BCIs. Security was already baked into the lab expectation.

Process

I dug into the realm of BCI security, narrowed down to BCI authentication, and read. A lot. I had to understand the state of the art, then the science underneath it, and then the math underneath that, which turned out to be highly relevant.

IoT TFNA itself is simple to state:

  • We can identify, classify, and discriminate a brain signal read through EEG as one motor imagery out of a set — a user imagining rotating their hand at the wrist versus rotating their foot at the joint.
  • We can also authenticate a user by having them think a thought password, differentiating their unique “mind-print” (mind finger print) from others.
  • Lets can we build a system on that conjuction!

IoT TFNA uses a single thought command to send a secure instruction to an IoT device inside the same packet used for authentication. A randomized unique token adds an extra layer of security between source and endpoint.

IoT TFNA started as an effort to extend the state of the art. Then it became the way I got to dig into my own dreams via the industry interest I was begining to garner.

Result

The poster edition was accepted to the 2019 IEEE SafeThings Workshop, where I presented to an audience of guests from industry and academia. It is my first lead author papers to go on to publication - all during my undergrad career.

Read the paper (PDF)

Where my head’s at now

In-ear EEG carries so much more information per signal than is utilized by the scientific community. Some fresh eyed startup should explore that… ;)
entry.summary: My first lead-authorship paper. One thought does two jobs at once: it proves who you are, and it tells the device what to do.

entry.title: My Greatest Accomplishment
entry.content:
Background and inspiration

I started producing around 2015 in Ableton, after taking a keen interest in expressing myself through music. A close friend — a certified genius — could riff his emotions on the piano effortlessly, and I was fascinated by it. Then I stumbled onto deadmau5’s streams, where he was producing live, and I was hooked.

By 2017 I had settled into my dorm at the University of Michigan, but I was missing a space where my expression felt at home. Turns out engineering campus has a few studios. I took the effort to get all the certifications required to use the rooms, and started renting hours.

Process

I never found my “workflow,” but I was obsessed with the pursuit of one — a black hole of never feeling qualified enough for authentic exploration.

Then one day, after a long one, I stopped trying to do it, and in frustration just began to riff.

I liked using sequencers. I liked my synth. I had small chains of workflow that made nice sounds reliably. So — why not plug this here, and this into that, and how about I just fuckin—

And bam.

Out of a chaotic mess layered from chaotic pieces, I found a emergent and pleasant sounding order - and it was representative of exactly what I had just discovered… completely self-referentially.

Result

An intro to a song. Disorganized noises, each with its own inspired idea, rushing together toward the angst, arriving at an order discovered by simply moving forward.

I titled the file on my machine my greatest accomplishment.

Where my head’s at now

I think it represents structured beauty emerging — or showing itself — out of the entropy.

The universe has a law to resolve itself, at least it seems that way. It is a gift to be part of its dance, and it may just be physically impossible not to be.
entry.summary: The file name I from a track I made at a University of Michigan studio

entry.title: Physics 2 PLTL: Teaching the Question Before the Equation

link.title: Physics 2 PLTL: Teaching the Question Before the Equation

entry.content:
Background and inspiration

During 2016 I became a Peer Academic Leader (PAL) at the STEM lab on Miami Dade College’s Wolfson Campus. After a semester of tutoring, I was hired to lead the Peer-Led Tutoring Lessons (PLTL) sessions for my Physics 2 professor.

It was my first experience lecturing — standing in front of a classroom and teaching for an hour. I made lesson plans, practiced every morning, and felt the nerves and the imposter syndrome like a true leader.

Process

I found that, like the lessons from the programming experience I was beginning to gain, and the lessons learned from tutoring, there were two common lessons:

  1. there is nothing new under the sun
  2. learning the illusion of “genius” being perspective, liberates.

I taught students how I personally learned:

  1. Discover the wording of the question you are actually trying to ask.
  2. Understand the perspective of the original innovator who asked it.
  3. See the beauty.

Physics2PLTL was a site dedicated to that process. On it I built a logic tree that took students from the homework I assigned to the answers, using the same resources I had used to get there.

Take flux, torque, current, gravitational attraction. As a list of equations, they are overwhelming. But once you learn that each of those calculations came out of a context — and that out from perspective from the science that came before it — a student can sit inside the point of view of Newton or Ampère and see the real beauty of science, and of the equation distilled from it.

Result

All of my students passed Physics 2.

The site kept drawing traffic for years afterward, and I received a couple of emails from strangers thanking me for the resources.

Around 2019 I stopped keeping up with the Squarespace account, and the site was seemingly purged. Rebuilding that logic tree here is on my list.

entry.title: Building a Farnsworth Fusor
entry.content:
Background and inspiration

During my Physics 2 honors class, I took it upon myself to complete a dream my brother and I had talked about: let’s build a fusion reactor.

At Miami Dade College, honors courses are evaluated with a capstone project — one that demonstrates mastery of the course material and challenges students to step up to the plate on their own interests in it. This was the excuse I needed.

Fusion was one of the bundle of “human” problems I took an interest in early in my educational journey. As I wrote in the background to IoT TFNA, it was also an apparent prerequisite for the dream of building a mecha. Building one that simply worked, as exposure to the disciplines involved, was more than enough for a capstone.

Process

I took my inspiration from the design published in Make: magazine, Vol. 36 — producing the CAD files, milling the materials, and building out the circuitry as required.

A Farnsworth fusor is an inertial electrostatic confinement device: a grid held at high negative voltage inside a vacuum chamber accelerates deuterium ions inward until some fraction of them collide hard enough to fuse.

A fusor operates at voltages and produces radiation that make it genuinely hazardous. Mine was built as coursework under supervision, and this post is a retrospective rather than a build guide.

Result

I logged much of the process on 3 short video, and edited them together now.
